title: Mental Maths Practice: Five Minutes a Day That Add Up
description: Simple daily routines for building quick mental maths, with ideas you can try today and a free game to make practice fun.
body:
Mental maths is a skill that grows with short, regular sessions. Five focused minutes each day builds more confidence than one long weekend marathon, because the brain loves repetition spread over time. Here is a friendly routine you can start today.

Start with numbers you already know

Begin each session with facts that feel comfortable. If 2s, 5s and 10s come easily, run through them first. A warm start builds momentum and puts you in a confident mood before the bigger facts arrive.

Keep sessions short and focused

Choose one small goal per session, such as the 6 times table or doubling numbers up to 50. A narrow target lets you notice progress quickly. When the goal feels easy, move the target up a notch.

Say the answer out loud

Speaking an answer such as "six times seven is forty two" connects sound, rhythm and memory. Parents and teachers can ask a quick question during daily moments: while walking, cooking or waiting for a bus. Seven times eight is a great question for a queue.

Break big problems into friendly pieces

Mental maths often means splitting a problem into easier parts. For 7 times 14, work out 7 times 10 and 7 times 4, then add 70 and 28 to reach 98. For 9 times 6, start with 10 times 6 equals 60, then take away 6 to land on 54. Practising these splits makes larger numbers feel manageable.

Mix operations to stay sharp

Multiplication, division, addition and subtraction are connected. If you know 6 times 7 equals 42, then 42 divided by 6 equals 7 and 42 minus 6 equals 36. Moving between these links helps facts stick and shows how numbers relate to each other.

Use a timer for gentle challenge

A friendly clock adds energy. Try a set number of questions and see how quickly you finish, then beat your own time tomorrow. Compare with yourself, since your own progress is the score that counts.

Practise with Multiplication Master

Multiplication Master is a free browser game that turns this routine into play. Each level shows an equation like 6 × 7 = 42, and you tap numbers on the board to fill it in. Levels come in two styles: finish a set number of equations, or score as much as you can before a three minute timer ends. Your score earns stars, and enough stars unlock further levels.

The Easy difficulty begins with small numbers, then grows to larger ranges, and includes subtraction versions of the same board so you can practise the links between operations. Some levels use decimals and negative numbers, which is a fun way to stretch your thinking once the basics feel solid.

A simple weekly plan

  • Monday: warm up with a table you know well, then play one level.
  • Tuesday: pick one new table and say each fact aloud.
  • Wednesday: play a timed level and note your score.
  • Thursday: practise splitting larger numbers into tens and ones.
  • Friday: replay your favourite level and aim for another star.

Small steps, repeated often, build real fluency. Ready to begin? Play Multiplication Master free and take your first level in seconds.

title: Learning Times Tables: A Friendly Step by Step Guide
description: A practical path through the times tables, from easy tables to the tricky ones, with tips for parents, teachers and learners.
body:
Times tables open the door to fractions, division, algebra and everyday calculations. The good news is that learning them can be calm and enjoyable when you follow a sensible order and practise a little each day.

Follow an gentle to advanced order

Start with the tables that have clear patterns, then build up to the bigger ones.

  • Tens: add a zero. 10 times 8 is 80.
  • Twos: double the number. 2 times 7 is 14.
  • Fives: the answers end in 0 or 5, and they match the minutes on a clock face.
  • Fours: double, then double again. 4 times 6 means 6, 12, 24.
  • Threes, sixes and nines come next, followed by sevens and eights.

Use the swap rule to halve the work

Multiplication works in both directions: 3 times 8 gives the same answer as 8 times 3. Once you know 3 times 8 equals 24, you also know 8 times 3. This means that by the time you reach the sevens, you already know 7 times 2, 7 times 3, 7 times 4, 7 times 5 and 7 times 6 from earlier tables. Only a handful of new facts remain, with 7 times 8 equals 56 being a favourite to chant.

Spot patterns in the nines

The digits of each answer in the 9 times table add up to 9: 18, 27, 36, 45 and so on. The tens digit goes up by one each step while the ones digit goes down by one. Spotting this makes the nines a joy to learn.

Connect multiplication and division

Every multiplication fact comes with a division partner. Knowing 6 times 7 equals 42 means you also know 42 divided by 6 equals 7 and 42 divided by 7 equals 6. Practise both directions together so each fact is learned as a small family of numbers.

Little and often beats long and rare

Five to ten minutes a day is a wonderful target. Choose one table, recite it, then test a few facts in random order. Random order matters because it checks that the answers are truly remembered, rather than recited as a song.

Make practice playful

Games keep motivation high. In Multiplication Master you see an equation board, for example 6 × 7 = 42, and tap numbers to complete it. Easy levels use smaller number ranges so you can build confidence, and a star rating shows how well you did on each level. Because you earn stars by scoring, replaying a level to beat your own result is a natural way to practise the same facts again.

The game also has timed levels lasting three minutes, which suit learners who enjoy a challenge, and levels with a set number of equations for those who prefer a steady pace. Pick whichever style matches your mood.

Celebrate progress

Keep a simple chart of tables you have mastered and colour one in whenever you feel confident. Praise effort and improvement, and revisit earlier tables occasionally so they stay fresh.

When you are ready for some practice, play Multiplication Master for free. It runs in your browser, so you can start right away on a phone, tablet or computer.

title: Multiplication Tricks That Make Big Numbers Feel Small
description: Handy multiplication tricks for 9s, 11s, 5s and bigger numbers, with worked examples you can try in your head.
body:
Multiplication tricks are shortcuts that turn big looking problems into quick, friendly steps. Here are several you can use straight away, each with an example.

Multiply by 10, 100 and 1000

Shift the digits left and fill with zeros. 34 times 10 is 340, and 34 times 100 is 3400. Decimals work the same way: 3.4 times 10 is 34.

Multiply by 5

Multiply by 10, then halve the result. For 5 times 18, take 10 times 18 equals 180, then half of that is 90.

Multiply by 9

Multiply by 10, then subtract the number once. For 9 times 7, take 70 and subtract 7 to reach 63. For 9 times 15, take 150 and subtract 15 to reach 135.

Multiply by 11 for two digit numbers

Add the two digits and place the total between them. For 11 times 23, add 2 and 3 to get 5, so the answer is 253. When the digits total 10 or more, carry the 1 into the first digit: for 11 times 78, 7 plus 8 is 15, so the answer is 858.

Multiply by 4 and 8

Double, then double again for 4. For 4 times 17, double to get 34, then double to get 68. For 8, double three times: 8 times 6 means 12, 24, 48.

Break a number into tens and ones

This works for almost any problem. For 7 times 16, split 16 into 10 and 6. Then 7 times 10 is 70 and 7 times 6 is 42, and 70 plus 42 gives 112.

Square numbers ending in 5

Take the tens digit, multiply it by the next number up, and attach 25. For 35 squared, 3 times 4 is 12, so the answer is 1225. For 65 squared, 6 times 7 is 42, so the answer is 4225.

Round and adjust

Choose a friendly nearby number, calculate, then correct. For 19 times 6, think 20 times 6 equals 120, then subtract 6 to reach 114. This approach shines whenever a number sits close to a multiple of ten.

Check answers with estimation

A quick estimate keeps you on track. For 48 times 6, round 48 to 50, so the answer should sit near 300. The true answer, 288, is close, which confirms the result looks right.

Combine tricks for bigger problems

Tricks work well as a team. For 12 times 15, split 12 into 10 and 2: 10 times 15 is 150 and 2 times 15 is 30, giving 180. For 25 times 8, double and halve: 25 times 8 equals 50 times 4 equals 100 times 2, which is 200. Choosing the trick that fits the numbers is a skill in itself, and it grows every time you practise.

Practise one trick a day

Pick a single trick each day and use it on five problems from around you, such as prices, page numbers or the number plates you pass. By the end of the week you will own a full toolkit.

Put the tricks to work

Tricks become second nature through repetition. Multiplication Master gives you a playful place to do that: each level presents an equation such as 6 × 7 = 42 on a tap the numbers board. Easy levels use small ranges to build speed, timed three minute levels reward quick thinking, and your score earns stars. Try the splitting and rounding ideas above while you play, and see how much faster your answers arrive.

Ready to test your new skills? Play Multiplication Master free and enjoy a few quick rounds.
